name: IBPS SO (Specialist Officer)
tagline: Specialist officer posts (IT, Agriculture, Law, HR, Marketing, Rajbhasha) in public sector banks

overview.about: IBPS conducts the CRP for Specialist Officers (Scale I) in public sector banks: IT Officer, Agricultural Field Officer, Law Officer, HR/Personnel Officer, Marketing Officer and Rajbhasha Adhikari. Prelims tests general aptitude; Mains is a Professional Knowledge test in your specialisation; then an interview.
eligibility: Post-specific degree: e.g. IT Officer — 4-year engineering degree in CS/IT/ECE etc. or PG in these fields; AFO — 4-year degree in agriculture/allied fields; Law — LLB with Bar Council enrolment; HR/Marketing — PG/MBA in the field; Rajbhasha — PG in Hindi/Sanskrit with English at graduation
Age 20–30 years (e.g. as on 01.07.2025 for the 2025 cycle); relaxation: SC/ST 5 yrs, OBC-NCL 3 yrs, PwBD 10 yrs
Indian citizen (or other categories as defined)
Check the exact degree list for your post in the notification

Law Officer and Rajbhasha Adhikari instead of Quant; total 150 Q / 125 marks / 120 min

chapters.title: Strategy: Prelims as a filter, PK as the decider

cards.title: Where rank is made
cards.body: Prelims is qualifying, but its sections are long (50 Q each). Mains has only **60 PK questions in 45 minutes**, so a few marks separate hundreds of candidates. Your **specialisation** depth decides the rank, with the interview adding 20%.

cards.title: English carries half marks
cards.body: In Prelims, English has 50 questions for **25 marks** (0.5 each). Clear its cut-off, but put extra effort into Reasoning and Quant/GA, each worth 50 marks.

cards.title: PK preparation
cards.body: Use standard textbooks of your degree, focusing on topics IBPS repeats: for IT — DBMS, networking, OS, security; for AFO — agronomy, soil science, horticulture, animal husbandry and agri-schemes; for HR — labour laws and HRM; for Marketing — 4Ps, segmentation, digital marketing.

cards.title: Rajbhasha Adhikari
cards.body: Mains for Rajbhasha has **45 objective + 2 descriptive** questions (translation/essay). The Prelims includes GA instead of Quant, like the Law Officer post.

cards.q: In IBPS SO Prelims, how many marks does the English section carry?
For which IBPS SO posts is Quant replaced by General Awareness in Prelims?
cards.explain: Law Officer and Rajbhasha Adhikari take GA (banking) instead of Quant.

notes.h: Exam structure and where rank is made
notes.p:
IBPS SO recruits specialist officers: **IT Officer, Agricultural Field Officer (AFO), Rajbhasha Adhikari, Law Officer, HR/Personnel Officer and Marketing Officer**. The process is **Prelims → Mains → Interview**.

**Prelims** is qualifying. For IT, AFO, HR and Marketing it has **English (50 Q, 25 marks), Reasoning (50 Q, 50 marks) and Quant (50 Q, 50 marks)**. For **Law Officer and Rajbhasha Adhikari**, Quant is replaced by **General Awareness with special reference to banking**.

**Mains** is the **Professional Knowledge (PK)** test, typically **60 questions in 45 minutes** (Rajbhasha has 45 objective + 2 descriptive questions). With so few questions, a handful of marks separates hundreds of candidates. The **final merit** combines Mains and the interview in **80 : 20** (check the latest notification).

notes.h: Prelims plan: clear cut-offs, don't over-invest
notes.p:
English carries only **0.5 marks per question**, so aim to clear its cut-off efficiently and invest more in Reasoning and Quant/GA, each worth 50 marks.

**Worked example: marks per question**
English: 25 ÷ 50 = **0.5**.
Reasoning: 50 ÷ 50 = **1**.
Quant or GA: 50 ÷ 50 = **1**.
A wrong English answer costs 0.5 × ¼ = **0.125**; a wrong Reasoning answer costs **0.25**. Accuracy matters in both, but each correct Reasoning answer is worth twice an English answer.
Use standard textbooks from your degree and focus on topics IBPS repeats.
points: **IT:** DBMS and SQL, networking and OSI, operating systems, data structures, software engineering, cyber security.
**AFO:** agronomy, soil science, horticulture, animal husbandry, fisheries, agri-economics, government agri-schemes, agri-credit.
**HR:** labour laws (including the labour codes), HRM functions, training, performance appraisal, industrial relations.
**Marketing:** 4Ps, segmentation–targeting–positioning, consumer behaviour, digital marketing, bank product marketing.
**Law:** banking laws, contract, negotiable instruments, SARFAESI, IBC, RBI and banking regulation.
**Rajbhasha:** official language policy, translation (Hindi ↔ English), essay writing.

notes.p:
Weeks 1–6: cover the full PK syllabus once, making one-page notes per topic.
Weeks 7–9: solve previous-year PK questions and topic-wise MCQs; note weak areas.
Weeks 10–11: full-length 60-question PK mocks (45 minutes) three times a week.
Week 12: revise notes and errors only; no new topics.

Run Prelims practice in parallel (1 hour daily) because Prelims must still be cleared.
Avoid these.
points: Preparing only for Prelims and leaving PK until after the result.
Spending equal time on English and Reasoning despite different marks.
Studying PK from random notes instead of standard textbooks.
Ignoring banking-related applications of your specialisation (e.g. agri-credit for AFO, cyber security for IT).

notes.p: Key points.
points: Prelims: English 50 Q/25 marks; Reasoning and Quant (or GA) 50 marks each.
Law and Rajbhasha: GA replaces Quant.
Mains: PK, about 60 Q in 45 min; Rajbhasha has descriptive questions too.
Final: Mains + interview (80 : 20).
Start PK from day one.

Normal forms: 1NF atomic values → 2NF no partial dependency → 3NF no transitive dependency → BCNF
ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
SQL: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DCL (GRANT, REVOKE)

cards.title: Security
cards.body: **Symmetric** encryption uses one key (AES, DES); **asymmetric** uses a public–private key pair (RSA). **Hashing** (SHA-256) is one-way. **SQL injection** and **XSS** are web attacks; **DDoS** floods a service.

cards.title: High-yield topics
cards.body: SQL query output questions, normal-form identification, subnetting basics, OSI layer of a device/protocol, and data-structure complexity (binary search O(log n), quicksort average O(n log n)).

cards.q: Which normal form removes transitive dependency?
cards.explain: 3NF requires no non-key attribute to depend on another non-key attribute (no transitive dependency).

cards.q: At which OSI layer does a router mainly operate?
cards.explain: Routers forward packets using IP addresses: layer 3, the Network layer.

cards.q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
cards.explain: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits; IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.

notes.p: DBMS is the most heavily tested IT area.
points: **Keys:** primary key (unique, not null), candidate key (any minimal unique key), foreign key (refers to another table's primary key), super key (any set that uniquely identifies rows).
**Normal forms:** 1NF (atomic values) → 2NF (no partial dependency on part of a composite key) → 3NF (no transitive dependency) → BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key).
**ACID:** Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
**SQL types:** DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE), DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DCL (GRANT, REVOKE), TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).
**Joins:** INNER (matching rows only), LEFT (all left rows), RIGHT, FULL OUTER.

notes.p:
Table EMP:
(1, 'Asha', 'IT', 50000), (2, 'Ravi', 'HR', 40000), (3, 'Meera', 'IT', 60000), (4, 'Kiran', 'HR', 45000), (5, 'Sohan', 'Ops', 30000)

Query: SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM EMP GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
Step 1 (group): IT → 50000, 60000; HR → 40000, 45000; Ops → 30000.
Step 2 (HAVING COUNT > 1): IT (2 rows) ✓, HR (2) ✓, Ops (1) ✗.
Step 3 (average): IT = (50000 + 60000) ÷ 2 = **55000**; HR = (40000 + 45000) ÷ 2 = **42500**.
Output: two rows — IT 55000, HR 42500.
Remember: **WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping**.

OSI has 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Hub = layer 1, switch = layer 2, router = layer 3. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and fast. IPv4 = 32 bits; IPv6 = 128 bits.

**Worked example: subnet 192.168.1.0/26.**
Host bits = 32 − 26 = 6 → addresses per subnet = 2⁶ = **64**; usable hosts = 64 − 2 = **62** (network and broadcast addresses excluded).
Subnet mask: /26 → 255.255.255.**192** (128 + 64).
Subnets: .0, .64, .128, .192.
First subnet: network 192.168.1.0, usable .1 to .62, broadcast **.63**.
points: IPv4 classes: A 1–126, B 128–191, C 192–223 (127 is loopback).

notes.p: These topics give quick, factual questions.
points: **Deadlock conditions (all four needed):** mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait.
**Scheduling:** FCFS, SJF (minimum average waiting time), Round Robin (time quantum), Priority.
**Paging** avoids external fragmentation; **thrashing** = too much paging, too little work.
**Stack:** LIFO; **queue:** FIFO.
**Complexities:** binary search O(log n); bubble/insertion sort O(n²); merge sort O(n log n) always; quicksort O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst.
Binary search on 1,024 sorted items needs at most ⌊log₂ 1024⌋ + 1 = **11** comparisons.

notes.p:
**Symmetric** encryption uses one shared key (AES, DES). **Asymmetric** uses a public–private key pair (RSA, ECC). **Hashing** (SHA-256) is one-way and used for integrity and password storage. A **digital signature** is created with the sender's private key and verified with the public key.

Web attacks: **SQL injection** (malicious SQL through input fields; prevented by parameterised queries), **XSS** (malicious scripts in web pages), **CSRF** (forged requests from a logged-in user), **DDoS** (flooding a service).
Last-day list.
points: 3NF removes transitive dependency; BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.
WHERE before grouping; HAVING after grouping.
/26 → 64 addresses, 62 usable, mask .192.
Router L3, switch L2, hub L1.
Four deadlock conditions.
Quicksort worst O(n²); merge sort O(n log n).
Symmetric = AES/DES; asymmetric = RSA.

cards.title: Crop seasons
points: Kharif (sown June–July with monsoon): rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut
Rabi (sown Oct–Dec): wheat, mustard, gram, barley
Zaid (short summer season): watermelon, cucumber, moong

cards.title: Soils of India
points: Alluvial: most widespread; Indo-Gangetic plains
Black (regur): cotton; high moisture retention
Red: low nitrogen; Deccan plateau
Laterite: leached, acidic; tea, coffee, cashew

cards.title: Revolutions
cards.body: **Green** (food grains, HYV seeds; M.S. Swaminathan), **White** (milk; Operation Flood 1970, Verghese Kurien), **Blue** (fisheries), **Yellow** (oilseeds), **Golden** (horticulture/honey), **Silver** (eggs/poultry).

cards.title: Key schemes
cards.body: **PM-KISAN**: ₹6,000/year in three instalments to landholding farmers. **PMFBY** (2016): crop insurance; farmer premium 2% kharif, 1.5% rabi, 5% commercial/horticulture. **Soil Health Card** (2015). **e-NAM** (2016): online agri market.

cards.title: AFO and the bank
cards.body: As AFO you appraise **agri loans**: KCC, farm mechanisation, dairy, poultry, warehouse loans. Know the scale of finance concept, the unit cost approach, and that NABARD refinances these loans.

cards.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
cards.explain: Wheat is sown in winter (Oct–Dec) and harvested in spring: a rabi crop.

cards.q: Under PMFBY, the farmer's premium for kharif food and oilseed crops is:
cards.explain: 2% for kharif, 1.5% for rabi, 5% for commercial/horticultural crops.

cards.q: Which soil is best known for cotton cultivation?
cards.explain: Black soil retains moisture and is ideal for cotton.

notes.p: India has three cropping seasons.
points: **Kharif** (sown June–July with the monsoon, harvested Sept–Oct): rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, soybean, groundnut, arhar.
**Rabi** (sown Oct–Dec, harvested March–April): wheat, mustard, gram, barley, peas.
**Zaid** (short summer season between rabi and kharif): watermelon, cucumber, muskmelon, moong.
India is the world's largest producer of milk and pulses and among the top producers of rice and wheat (check the latest data).

notes.p: Know the soil, its features and its crops.
points: **Alluvial:** most widespread; Indo-Gangetic plains; fertile; rice, wheat, sugarcane.
**Black (regur):** high clay, retains moisture, cracks when dry; **cotton**.
**Red:** red due to iron oxide; low in nitrogen; Deccan plateau.
**Laterite:** leached and acidic; tea, coffee, cashew.
**Acidic soils** are corrected with **lime**; **alkaline/sodic soils** with **gypsum**.
Ideal NPK use ratio is commonly cited as **4 : 2 : 1**.

notes.p:
Fertiliser grades show nutrient percentage: **urea 46% N**, **DAP 18% N and 46% P₂O₅**, **MOP 60% K₂O**, **SSP 16% P₂O₅**.

**Worked example 1:** How much urea supplies 60 kg of nitrogen?
Urea needed = 60 ÷ 0.46 = **130.4 kg** (about 130 kg).
Check: 130.4 × 0.46 = 60.0 ✓.

**Worked example 2:** A field needs 46 kg P₂O₅ and 40 kg N. DAP is applied first.
DAP for P = 46 ÷ 0.46 = **100 kg** → this also supplies 100 × 0.18 = 18 kg N.
Remaining N = 40 − 18 = 22 kg → urea = 22 ÷ 0.46 ≈ **47.8 kg**.
Always supply the nutrient available from only one source (here P from DAP) first, then top up the others.

notes.h: KCC limit: scale of finance method
notes.p:
As AFO you appraise **agri loans**. For crop loans under KCC, the first-year short-term limit is worked out as: **scale of finance × area cultivated + 10% for post-harvest/household/consumption needs + 20% for repairs and maintenance of farm assets + crop insurance and asset insurance premium**. The limit is usually raised each later year for cost escalation; check the current RBI master circular on KCC.

**Worked example:** Scale of finance for a crop = ₹40,000 per acre; farmer cultivates 2 acres; insurance premium = ₹2,000.
Crop component = 40,000 × 2 = ₹80,000.
+10% = ₹8,000. +20% = ₹16,000. + insurance ₹2,000.
First-year limit = 80,000 + 8,000 + 16,000 + 2,000 = **₹1,06,000**.
Frequently asked facts.
points: **Green** (food grains, HYV seeds; M.S. Swaminathan); **White** (milk; Operation Flood 1970, Verghese Kurien); **Blue** (fisheries); **Yellow** (oilseeds); **Golden** (horticulture/honey); **Silver** (eggs/poultry).
**PM-KISAN:** ₹6,000 a year in three instalments to landholding farmer families.
**PMFBY (2016):** crop insurance; farmer premium 2% kharif, 1.5% rabi, 5% commercial/horticultural crops.
**Soil Health Card (2015)**, **e-NAM (2016)** online mandi, **PMKSY** (micro-irrigation: 'More crop per drop').
Seed chain: nucleus → breeder (golden-yellow tag) → foundation (white tag) → certified (blue tag).
MSP is announced by the Government on the recommendation of the **CACP**.

notes.p: Last-day list.
points: Kharif: rice, cotton, soybean; Rabi: wheat, mustard, gram; Zaid: melons, moong.
Black soil → cotton; acidic soil → lime; sodic soil → gypsum.
Urea 46% N; DAP 18-46-0; MOP 60% K₂O; SSP 16% P₂O₅.
KCC limit = SoF × area + 10% + 20% + insurance.
PMFBY premiums 2% / 1.5% / 5%.
Breeder tag golden-yellow, foundation white, certified blue.

notes.p: IBPS SO IT Officer Mains PK covers DBMS, networking, operating systems, data structures, software engineering, computer organisation, web technologies, cloud and security. This chapter covers the topics not in the IT essentials chapter: data structures and algorithms, software engineering, web and cloud.

**Linear:** arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues. **Non-linear:** trees (binary, BST, AVL, B-trees for databases), graphs (BFS uses a queue, DFS uses a stack/recursion), heaps (priority queues), hash tables.

**Worked example 1 (stack):** Evaluate the postfix expression 5 3 + 2 *.
Push 5, push 3; "+" pops 3 and 5 → push 8; push 2; "*" pops 2 and 8 → push **16**.

**Worked example 2 (binary search):** In a sorted list of 1,024 records, binary search needs at most log₂1,024 = **10** comparisons (plus one for the final check in some implementations), versus up to 1,024 for linear search.

The **SDLC** runs through requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance. **Waterfall** is linear; **Agile** delivers in sprints with user feedback; **DevOps** integrates development and operations with continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD).

**Coupling** (dependence between modules) should be low; **cohesion** (focus within a module) should be high. **COCOMO** estimates effort from lines of code. **Cyclomatic complexity** = E − N + 2P for a control-flow graph — the number of independent paths.

**Worked example 3:** A control-flow graph has 9 edges, 7 nodes and 1 connected component. Cyclomatic complexity = 9 − 7 + 2 = **4** → at least 4 test cases for path coverage.

HTML structures pages, CSS styles them, JavaScript adds behaviour. HTTP methods: GET (retrieve), POST (create), PUT (replace), DELETE. Status codes: 200 OK, 301 moved, 404 not found, 500 server error. **REST APIs** exchange JSON over HTTP; banks expose APIs for UPI, account aggregation and partner integration.

**Cloud:** IaaS (virtual machines), PaaS (managed platforms), SaaS (applications). Benefits: scalability and pay-per-use; concerns for banks: data localisation, vendor lock-in and outsourcing risk — governed by RBI’s IT outsourcing directions.
points: Virtualisation: hypervisor runs multiple VMs on one host.
Containers share the host OS kernel (e.g. Docker).

notes.p:
**Number representation:** two’s complement for signed integers; IEEE 754 for floating point. **Memory hierarchy:** registers → cache (L1/L2/L3) → RAM → SSD/HDD. **Cache mapping:** direct, associative, set-associative. **Pipelining** overlaps instruction stages; hazards are structural, data and control.

**Worked example 4:** A 4-stage pipeline with 1 ns per stage runs 100 instructions in (4 + 100 − 1) = **103 ns**, versus 400 ns without pipelining — a speed-up of about 3.9.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: BFS uses a queue; DFS a stack.
Quicksort worst case is O(n²).
Low coupling, high cohesion is the goal.
Overloading is compile-time; overriding is run-time.

cards.title: DSCR
cards.body: Debt Service Coverage Ratio = (net profit + depreciation + interest) ÷ (instalment + interest). Banks usually look for an average DSCR of about 1.5 for agri term loans.

cards.q: Blast is a major fungal disease of:
Which buffalo breed is known for the highest milk yield in India?
A project has annual cash available for debt service of ₹1.5 lakh and annual debt service of ₹1 lakh. DSCR is:

notes.p: The AFO Professional Knowledge paper covers agronomy, soils, horticulture, plant protection, animal husbandry, fisheries, agricultural engineering, agri economics and finance, and government schemes. This chapter adds plant protection, horticulture, livestock breeds and project appraisal to the AFO essentials chapter.

Crop losses come from insects, diseases and weeds. **Fungal** diseases are the most common (rusts and smuts of wheat, blast and sheath blight of rice, late blight of potato — the cause of the Irish famine). **Bacterial** diseases include bacterial leaf blight of rice. **Viral** diseases are spread by vectors such as whiteflies and aphids.

**IPM** combines resistant varieties, cultural practices, traps, bio-control (Trichogramma against borers; Trichoderma against soil fungi; NPV against caterpillars) and need-based pesticide use. Pesticide labels carry colour-coded toxicity triangles: red (extremely toxic), yellow, blue, green (least toxic).

Horticulture covers fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation and medicinal crops. Vegetative propagation (grafting in mango, budding in citrus and rose) keeps true-to-type plants. **Protected cultivation** extends seasons and raises yields of high-value crops.

Livestock: India has many indigenous breeds — **Gir** and **Sahiwal** (dairy cattle), **Murrah** (buffalo), **Marwari** (horse), **Jamunapari** and **Beetal** (goats). Crossbreeding with **Holstein Friesian** and **Jersey** raises yields but needs better feed and care. The **National Animal Disease Control Programme** vaccinates against foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis.

An AFO appraises technical feasibility, economic viability and bankability.

**Worked example 1 (dairy unit):** Cost ₹5 lakh; margin 25% (₹1.25 lakh) from the farmer; bank loan ₹3.75 lakh over 5 years at 10%. Year-1 interest ≈ ₹37,500; principal instalment ₹75,000 → debt service ≈ ₹1.125 lakh. If net income + depreciation + interest = ₹1.8 lakh, DSCR = 1.8 ÷ 1.125 = **1.6** — acceptable.

**Worked example 2 (crop loan by scale of finance):** Scale of finance for paddy ₹60,000/ha; farmer grows 2 ha. Crop component = **₹1.2 lakh**; KCC limits then add post-harvest/household needs (10%) and farm-asset maintenance (20%) per RBI–NABARD norms.
points: BCR (benefit–cost ratio) > 1 indicates viability.

notes.p:
**Farm machinery:** primary tillage (mould-board plough, disc plough), secondary tillage (harrow, cultivator, rotavator), sowing (seed drill, zero-till drill), harvesting (combine harvester, reaper). **Post-harvest losses** are high for fruits and vegetables; cold chains, pack-houses and processing cut losses.

**Soil and water conservation structures:** contour bunds, terraces, check dams, farm ponds. **Worked recall example:** a zero-till drill sows wheat directly into rice stubble, saving time and reducing stubble burning.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Rust is a wheat disease; blast is rice.
Murrah is buffalo; Gir and Sahiwal are cattle.
DSCR includes interest in both numerator and denominator.
Red triangle = most toxic pesticide.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Rice blast; wheat rust; potato late blight.
IPM: cultural, mechanical, biological, need-based chemical.
Grafting (mango), budding (citrus, rose).
Gir, Sahiwal, Murrah; HF and Jersey.
DSCR ≈ 1.5 for agri term loans.
Scale of finance → KCC limit.

cards.title: Recovery and resolution
points: RDB Act, 1993 (now RDBF) — Debt Recovery Tribunals for claims of ₹20 lakh and above
SARFAESI Act, 2002 — enforce security without court; 60-day demand notice (Sec 13(2))
IBC, 2016 — CIRP before NCLT; 180 days, extendable by 90; overall 330-day outer limit
Lok Adalats for small claims and settlements

cards.title: Other laws for bankers
points: PMLA, 2002 — KYC, record keeping, reporting to FIU-IND
NI Act, 1881 — Sec 138 cheque dishonour
FEMA, 1999 — foreign exchange
Limitation Act, 1963 — 3 years for most money claims; acknowledgment restarts the period

cards.title: SARFAESI essentials
cards.body: Applies to secured debts classified as **NPA**; not to agricultural land or loans below ₹1 lakh, or where the outstanding is less than 20% of principal and interest. After 60 days’ notice the bank may take possession (Sec 13(4)); borrowers may appeal to the DRT (Sec 17).

cards.title: Remember section numbers
cards.body: Sec 13(2) SARFAESI notice; Sec 14 assistance of CMM/DM; Sec 17 appeal to DRT. IBC: Sec 7 (financial creditor), Sec 9 (operational creditor), Sec 10 (corporate debtor itself).

cards.q: Under SARFAESI, the borrower is given a demand notice period of:
A financial creditor initiates CIRP under which section of the IBC?
cards.explain: Sec 9 operational creditor; Sec 10 corporate debtor.

cards.q: The pecuniary threshold for approaching a DRT is a debt of:
cards.explain: Raised from ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh in 2018.

notes.p: The Law Officer PK paper focuses on laws a bank’s legal department uses daily: banking regulation, recovery and insolvency, negotiable instruments, contracts and securities, KYC/AML, and consumer protection. Questions cite section numbers, so memorise the high-frequency ones.

The **RBI Act, 1934** constitutes the RBI and frames monetary policy (inflation targeting and the MPC under Chapter IIIF). The **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** governs licensing, capital, management, audits, directions (Sec 35A), removal of managerial persons (Sec 36AA), supersession of boards (Sec 36ACA) and moratorium/amalgamation (Sec 45). The **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020** extended RBI supervision over cooperative banks. The **Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025** allowed up to four nominees for deposit accounts and changed the "substantial interest" threshold — check the notified provisions.

**DRTs** under the RDB Act adjudicate bank claims of ₹20 lakh or more; appeals go to the **DRAT**. **SARFAESI** allows secured creditors to enforce security interest without court intervention after classifying the account as NPA.

**Worked example 1 (SARFAESI eligibility):** A loan of ₹50 lakh secured by a factory building, NPA since 4 months; outstanding ₹45 lakh. Not agricultural land, above ₹1 lakh, and outstanding exceeds 20% of principal + interest → SARFAESI **applies**. Steps: Sec 13(2) notice (60 days) → consider objections (reply within 15 days) → Sec 13(4) possession → valuation and auction.

**IBC**: CIRP must be completed within 180 days (extendable by 90), with an outer limit of 330 days including litigation; the minimum default to trigger CIRP is ₹1 crore (raised in 2020).

The **PMLA, 2002** and RBI’s KYC Master Direction require customer due diligence, periodic KYC updation, and reporting of cash transaction reports (CTR) and suspicious transaction reports (STR) to **FIU-IND**. The **Consumer Protection Act, 2019** and the **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021)** provide redress to bank customers.

**Worked example 2 (limitation):** A loan instalment fell due on 1 April 2022. The bank must file a recovery suit within 3 years — by 1 April 2025, since the day of default is excluded when computing the period — unless the borrower acknowledged the debt in writing within that period, which starts a fresh 3-year period from the acknowledgment.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: DRT threshold ₹20 lakh; IBC trigger ₹1 crore; SARFAESI minimum ₹1 lakh.
SARFAESI does not apply to agricultural land.
Sec 7 vs 9 vs 10 of the IBC.
Limitation is usually 3 years for money claims; 12 years for mortgage suits.

notes.p: Key points.
points: RBI Act 1934; BR Act 1949 (Sec 35A, 45).
RDB Act 1993 — DRT ≥ ₹20 lakh.
SARFAESI 2002 — Sec 13(2) 60 days; Sec 17 appeal.
IBC 2016 — 180 + 90 days; 330-day cap; ₹1 crore trigger.
PMLA 2002 — CTR/STR to FIU-IND.
Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021.

chapters.title: Law Officer PK: contracts, securities & banker–customer law

cards.title: Indian Contract Act, 1872
points: Valid contract: offer, acceptance, lawful consideration, competent parties, free consent, lawful object (Sec 10)
Minor’s agreement is void (Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, 1903)
Indemnity (Sec 124) vs guarantee (Sec 126): guarantee has three parties
Bailment (Sec 148); pledge (Sec 172) — bailment of goods as security

cards.title: Charges on security
points: Pledge — possession with the lender (goods, gold)
Hypothecation — possession with the borrower (vehicles, stock)
Mortgage — immovable property (Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Sec 58)
Lien — right to retain; banker’s general lien
Assignment — transfer of actionable claims (book debts, LIC policies)

cards.title: Types of mortgage (Sec 58 TPA)
points: Simple, usufructuary, English, conditional sale
Equitable mortgage (by deposit of title deeds) — notified towns
Anomalous mortgage — any other combination

cards.title: Banker–customer relationship
cards.body: Primarily **debtor–creditor** for deposits (reversed for loans), with additional roles: trustee, bailee (safe custody), agent (collecting cheques), lessor–lessee (lockers). Bankers owe a duty of secrecy subject to legal exceptions.

cards.title: Guarantor’s rights
cards.body: A surety’s liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor (Sec 128). A surety is discharged by variance in terms without consent (Sec 133) or release of the principal debtor (Sec 134).

cards.q: An agreement with a minor is:
A car loan where the vehicle stays with the borrower typically involves:
A contract of guarantee is defined in Section ___ of the Indian Contract Act:

notes.h: Why contract law matters to bankers
notes.p: Every loan, guarantee and security document is a contract. A Law Officer must check that documents are validly executed, that securities are properly created and registered, and that limitation is not missed. Questions frequently test definitions and leading case law.

**Sec 10** lists the essentials of a valid contract. Agreements without consideration are void except in Sec 25 cases (natural love and affection in writing and registered; compensation for past voluntary service; promise to pay a time-barred debt in writing).

A **contract of guarantee** (Sec 126) involves the creditor, the principal debtor and the surety. The surety’s liability is co-extensive (Sec 128), but the surety is discharged by variance without consent (Sec 133), release of the debtor (Sec 134) or the creditor’s act impairing the surety’s remedy (Sec 139).

**Worked example 1:** A bank extends a loan’s tenure and raises the rate without the guarantor’s consent. Under **Sec 133**, the guarantor is discharged for transactions after the variance. Banks therefore take guarantor consent for any material change.

**Pledge** — delivery of movable goods as security (gold loans). **Hypothecation** — charge on movables without possession; registered with the **ROC** for companies and with **CERSAI** for security interests. **Mortgage** — interest in immovable property; an **equitable mortgage** by deposit of title deeds is common in housing loans in notified towns. **Assignment** — of book debts or insurance policies.

**Worked example 2:** A company borrows working capital against stock. The bank takes **hypothecation**, files the charge with the ROC within the prescribed period, and registers it on **CERSAI** so later lenders can see the prior charge.

Relationships: **debtor–creditor** (deposits), **creditor–debtor** (loans), **bailor–bailee** (safe custody), **principal–agent** (collections), **lessor–lessee** (lockers). The banker’s **general lien** allows retaining securities for any debt due, unless an express contract excludes it. Secrecy exceptions (Tournier v. National Provincial Bank, 1924): compulsion by law, duty to the public, bank’s own interest, customer’s consent.
points: Garnishee order: court attaches funds of the judgment debtor held by the bank.
Right of set-off: combine accounts of the same customer in the same capacity.

notes.p: Under the **NI Act**, a holder in due course takes an instrument for value, before maturity, in good faith — and gets a better title than the transferor. **Sec 138** complaints require a demand notice within 30 days of the dishonour memo, 15 days for payment, and a complaint within one month after that. **Sec 143A** allows interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount. Endorsements may be blank, full, restrictive or conditional.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Indemnity has two parties; guarantee three.
Pledge needs possession; hypothecation does not.
Minor’s agreement: void, not voidable.
Tournier case: four exceptions to secrecy.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Sec 10 essentials; Sec 25 exceptions.
Sec 124 indemnity; 126 guarantee; 128 co-extensive; 133 variance.
Sec 148 bailment; 172 pledge.
TPA Sec 58: six types of mortgage.
CERSAI registration of security interests.
Tournier (1924): secrecy exceptions.

cards.title: HR functions
points: HR planning → recruitment → selection → induction
Training & development; career and succession planning
Performance management; compensation & benefits
Employee relations, grievance handling, discipline, separation

cards.title: Labour law framework
points: Four labour codes: Wages (2019); Industrial Relations, Social Security, OSH (2020)
IR Code: standing orders and prior permission for lay-off/retrenchment/closure above 300 workers (states may vary)
Social Security Code: EPF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit; covers gig and platform workers
Payment of gratuity: 15 days’ wages per completed year (after 5 years’ service under the old Act)

cards.title: Training evaluation and appraisal
points: Kirkpatrick: reaction → learning → behaviour → results
Appraisal: rating scales, MBO, BARS, 360-degree, assessment centre
Errors: halo, horns, leniency, central tendency, recency

cards.title: Industrial relations
cards.body: Collective bargaining, grievance redressal, conciliation, arbitration and adjudication (labour courts, tribunals). Banks negotiate wages industry-wide through **bipartite settlements** between IBA and unions.

cards.title: HR metrics
cards.body: Attrition rate = separations ÷ average headcount × 100. Cost per hire, time to hire, training hours per employee, absenteeism rate.

cards.q: Kirkpatrick’s four levels of training evaluation, in order, are:
Wage settlements in Indian public sector banks are decided mainly through:
options: bipartite settlements between IBA and unions

cards.q: A bank had 50 separations with an average headcount of 1,000. Annual attrition rate:

notes.p: The HR/Personnel Officer paper covers HRM concepts, HRD, performance management, compensation, industrial relations, labour laws, organisational behaviour and contemporary HR (HR analytics, employer branding, diversity). Answers are objective, so precise definitions and law details matter.

**Job analysis** produces a **job description** (duties) and **job specification** (qualities needed). Recruitment can be internal (promotions, transfers) or external (campus, exams like IBPS). Selection tools: tests, group discussions, interviews, reference checks. **Induction** integrates new hires.

**Training** methods: on-the-job (coaching, job rotation, apprenticeship) and off-the-job (lectures, case studies, simulations, e-learning). **Kirkpatrick’s model** evaluates reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

**Worked example 1:** A bank needs 120 clerks next year: 60 retirements, 40 new branches’ posts, and expected attrition of 2% on 1,000 staff (20). Requirement = 60 + 40 + 20 = **120** — confirming the plan.

Compensation includes basic pay, allowances (DA, HRA), incentives, and benefits (PF, gratuity, pension, medical). **Job evaluation** methods: ranking, grading, point-factor, factor comparison. **Performance-linked incentives** have been introduced in PSBs through bipartite settlements.

**Worked example 2 (gratuity, old Act formula):** Last drawn monthly wages ₹52,000; service 20 years. Gratuity = 15/26 × 52,000 × 20 = **₹6 lakh** (subject to the statutory ceiling of ₹20 lakh under the old Act; check provisions under the Social Security Code).

The **four labour codes** consolidated 29 central labour laws. The **IR Code** covers trade unions, standing orders, strikes (notice requirements) and dispute resolution; the **Social Security Code** covers EPF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit and gig workers; the **Code on Wages** sets a national floor wage and timely payment; the **OSH Code** covers safety, health and working conditions. Since state and central rules continue to evolve, verify current provisions.
points: Grievance procedure: immediate supervisor → department head → grievance committee → management.
Domestic enquiry: charge-sheet → reply → enquiry → findings → penalty, following natural justice.

notes.p:
**HR analytics** uses data on hiring, performance and attrition to predict risks and guide decisions. **Competency mapping** defines the skills each role needs. **Employee engagement** surveys and **employer branding** help retention. **Diversity and inclusion** policies, **POSH Act (2013)** compliance (Internal Committee in every office with 10 or more employees), and **hybrid work** arrangements are frequent interview topics.

**Worked example 3:** If annual attrition among new officers falls from 12% to 8% in a cohort of 2,500, the bank retains **100** more officers each year, saving recruitment and training costs.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Job description (job) vs job specification (person).
Kirkpatrick order: reaction, learning, behaviour, results.
Gratuity divisor is 26 (working days), with 15 days’ wages per year.
Conciliation ≠ arbitration (arbitration is binding).

notes.p: Key points.
points: HR cycle: plan, recruit, select, induct, train, appraise, reward, separate.
Four labour codes (2019–2020).
Kirkpatrick: four levels.
Gratuity = 15/26 × wages × years.
Attrition = separations ÷ average headcount.
Bipartite settlements set PSB wages.

Product life cycle: introduction, growth, maturity, decline
Maslow-based needs; wants; demand

SERVQUAL dimensions: reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness (RATER)
Service gaps model (Parasuraman, Zeithaml, Berry)

cards.title: Bank marketing
cards.body: Products: deposits, loans, cards, third-party products (insurance, mutual funds). Channels: branches, BCs, mobile, internet, DSAs. **CRM** tracks customer lifetime value; **cross-selling** sells additional products to existing customers.

cards.title: Digital marketing
cards.body: SEO, SEM, social media, content marketing, email. Metrics: CTR = clicks ÷ impressions; conversion rate = conversions ÷ visitors; CAC = marketing cost ÷ new customers.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of the original 4Ps?
cards.explain: People is an added P in services marketing.

cards.q: In the BCG matrix, a high-share product in a low-growth market is a:
An ad gets 50,000 impressions and 1,000 clicks. CTR is:

notes.p: The Marketing Officer paper covers marketing management fundamentals, consumer behaviour, product and pricing, distribution, promotion, services and bank marketing, CRM, digital marketing and market research. Questions are mostly conceptual with some calculations.

**Marketing** identifies and satisfies customer needs profitably. Philosophies have evolved: production → product → selling → marketing → **societal marketing**. **STP**: divide the market into segments (demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioural), choose target segments, and position the offering in customers’ minds.

**Worked example 1:** A bank designs a zero-balance salary account with free insurance for young IT employees in metros (demographic + geographic + behavioural segmentation) and positions it as "banking that moves at your speed".

**Product** levels: core benefit, actual product, augmented product. **PLC** strategies differ by stage — awareness in introduction, differentiation in maturity. **Pricing**: cost-plus, value-based, penetration (low entry price), skimming (high entry price), psychological (₹999).

**Worked example 2 (break-even):** A credit-card variant has fixed costs of ₹50 lakh a year, revenue of ₹2,500 per card and variable cost ₹1,500 per card. Break-even = 50,00,000 ÷ (2,500 − 1,500) = **5,000 cards**.

**Place**: distribution channels and coverage. **Promotion**: advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations, direct and digital marketing — the **IMC** approach keeps messages consistent.

Bank products are services, so quality depends on people and processes. **SERVQUAL** measures the gap between expected and perceived service on reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. **CRM** uses customer data to retain and grow relationships; retaining a customer is usually cheaper than acquiring one. **Customer lifetime value** guides how much to spend on acquisition.
points: Consumer decision process: need recognition → information search → evaluation → purchase → post-purchase behaviour.
AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action.

notes.p:
**Market research** process: define the problem → research design (exploratory, descriptive, causal) → data collection (primary via surveys, interviews, observation; secondary from reports) → sampling (probability: random, stratified, cluster; non-probability: convenience, quota, judgement) → analysis → report.

**Consumer behaviour** is shaped by cultural, social, personal and psychological factors. **Cognitive dissonance** after a purchase is reduced by reassurance and good after-sales service.

**Worked example 3:** A bank surveys 400 customers; 300 say they would recommend it, 60 are neutral and 40 would not. If promoters are 300 and detractors 40, a simple **Net Promoter Score** = (300 − 40) ÷ 400 × 100 = **65**.
Mix-ups to avoid.
points: Cash cow = high share, low growth; star = high share, high growth.
Skimming = high initial price; penetration = low.
SERVQUAL has five dimensions (RATER).
Ansoff diversification = new product + new market.

notes.p: Key points.
points: 4Ps + people, process, physical evidence.
STP; PLC four stages.
BCG, Ansoff, SWOT, Porter’s five forces.
SERVQUAL: RATER.
Break-even = fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit.
CTR, conversion rate, CAC.
